resumen: All living organisms are made of **cells**. Cells are so small that we need a **microscope** to **magnify** them.
## Parts of a plant cell
- **Cell wall**: strong and stiff, holds the cell in shape. Made of **cellulose**.
- **Cell membrane**: thin and flexible, lies inside the cell wall, controls what goes in and out.
- **Cytoplasm**: like clear jelly; chemical reactions that keep the cell alive happen here.
- **Nucleus**: controls the activities of the cell.
- **Sap vacuole**: large space filled with **cell sap** (sugars and other substances dissolved in water).
- **Chloroplasts**: where plants make their food (photosynthesis). Green because they contain **chlorophyll**.
- **Mitochondria** (singular: mitochondrion): energy is released from food.
## Microscopes
Parts: eyepiece, coarse and fine focussing knobs, objective lenses (low, medium, high power), stage, mirror.
To look at onion cells: put a thin layer of onion in a drop of water on a slide, lower a **cover slip** without air bubbles, start with the **smallest objective lens**, then focus.
Onion cells are not green because they have no chloroplasts (they grow underground, away from light).
A model of a cell has **strengths** and **limitations** (weaknesses).

resumen: All animals, including you, are made of cells (about 100 trillion in a person).
## Similarities with plant cells
Animal cells also have a **cell membrane**, **cytoplasm**, **mitochondria** and a **nucleus**.
## Differences
Animal cells do **not** have a cell wall, chloroplasts or a large sap vacuole. Their shape is often irregular or round.
## Looking at cheek cells
Rub a cotton bud inside your cheek, rub it on a slide, add a drop of **methylene blue**. It **stains** the cells blue so they are easier to see. Wear **safety glasses**.

resumen: Each kind of cell has a **function** (the job it does). A **specialised** cell has a structure that helps it do its function well: it is **adapted**.
## Specialised animal cells
- **Red blood cell**: carries oxygen. Small, to fit through tiny **capillaries**. Full of the red **pigment haemoglobin**, which carries oxygen. **No nucleus**, leaving more space for haemoglobin.
- **Neurone**: carries **electrical signals** around the body (e.g. from the brain to muscles). Long **axon** for fast signals; **dendrites** collect signals from other nerve cells.
- **Ciliated cell**: has tiny hairs called **cilia** that move. Lines the tubes to the lungs. Other cells make sticky **mucus** that traps dust and bacteria; cilia sweep it up to the mouth.
## Specialised plant cells
- **Root hair cell**: on the outside of roots; **absorbs** water from the soil. Long thin extension. No chloroplasts (no light underground).
- **Palisade cell**: in leaves; makes food by photosynthesis. Lots of **chloroplasts** with chlorophyll, which absorbs energy from sunlight.

resumen: Living things are called **organisms**.
## From cells to organisms
- **Tissue**: a group of similar cells working together to carry out a function. Examples: **onion epidermis**, **ciliated epithelium** (lines the tubes to the lungs).
- **Organ**: a structure made of several different tissues working together. Examples: brain, heart, stomach, muscles; in plants: leaves, roots, flowers.
- **Organ system**: a set of organs working together for the same function, e.g. the circulatory system (heart and blood vessels), digestive, respiratory, skeletal systems.
- A leaf contains an **upper epidermis**, **palisade layer**, **spongy layer** and **lower epidermis**.
## Cell discovery timeline
- 1625 Galileo builds the first microscope.
- 1665 Robert Hooke looks at cork and names the little compartments **cells**.
- 1670 Anton van Leeuwenhoek improves the microscope and sees living cells in pond water.
- 1833 Robert Brown discovers the nucleus in plant cells.
- 1838 Schleiden: all plant tissues are made of cells; Schwann: animal tissues too.
- 1845 Carl Heinrich Braun: cells are the basic unit of all life.
- 1855 Rudolf Virchow: all cells come only from other cells.
